arguments.text: Clean Up City Hall is a package of Props A, D, E and F to improve neighborhood services, speed up permitting and reduce wasteful spending so we can invest in our great city. PROPOSITION D GIVES MORE VOTERS A VOICE ON WHAT APPEARS ON BALLOTS. Currently a minority of supervisors, just 2% of voters or the mayor acting alone, can throw anything on the ballot without public input, transparency or proven community support. “Even well-intentioned ideas can include mistakes and unintended consequences.” - Ben Hur, former SF Ethics Chair. San Francisco is the only city in California that allows these low thresholds — and that’s why we have the longest and most confusing ballots in the state. PROP D REQUIRES MORE TRANSPARENCY, COMPROMISE & COMMUNITY INPUT. Proposition D requires a public vote of the majority of supervisors or signatures from 8% of voters. It removes the mayor’s sole authority to place measures on the ballot to ensure a fair balance of power. The signature requirement remains below the state standard of 10% and neighboring cities like Oakland. THE RESULT OF THESE MODEST REFORMS WILL BE MORE OPEN DEBATE AND CITIZEN PARTICIPATION BEFORE MEASURES ARE ON THE BALLOT. San Francisco works best when we work in coalitions together. Please join the citywide coalition to make the system accountable to all!

arguments.heading: No on D: It silences San Francisco voters
arguments.text: Proponents call it “modest reform.” A fourfold increase is not modest. It’s extreme. Quadrupling signature requirements from 10,600 to 42,500 will require hiring paid signature firms to qualify and cost one million dollars or more. That extreme cost will price out neighborhood groups, unions and community advocates from participating in the initiative process. Proponents have raised $8.6 million, collected from a small number of billionaires and venture capitalists. They can afford the higher costs. But the rest of us can’t. Ending citizen initiatives won’t move San Francisco forwards. Instead, it takes us back to 1898, when San Francisco became one of the first California cities to win this right. If this passes, San Francisco will have the highest signature requirement of any California county. Higher than Los Angeles and San Jose. Over three times higher than statewide measures which require 2.4%. Proponents want you to believe that raising the threshold from 2% to 8% is modest. But that’s like raising your rent from $2000 to $8000. It’s extreme – and extremely harmful. Don’t be fooled. Don’t rob our right to vote. Vote NO on D.

arguments.heading: NO ON D: DON’T ROB OUR RIGHT TO VOTE.
arguments.text: Don’t be fooled. This isn’t about streamlining or state standards. Prop D takes away rights San Franciscans have held for 125 years: to put citizen initiatives on the ballot. Robbing it away. San Francisco was the first California city to have this right. Now, wealthy tech billionaires are spending millions to take it away. They would quadruple the signatures required from 10,600 to 42,500, a limit so high only the very wealthy can reach it. Follow the money. Wealthy interests can afford to pay one million dollars to collect 42,500 signatures. Neighborhood groups, labor unions and community advocates will be priced out. We’ll lose our voice in the democratic process. 10,600 signatures is tough and fair. Since 1932, around 10,600 signatures have been required to qualify a measure. It’s not easy: citizen-initiatives are only 15% of all ballot measures. But when City Hall ignores us, citizens have the power to act. A check and balance. 42,500 signatures is out of reach. It will be impossible for citizen-led, grassroots organizations to qualify a measure. After 125 years, it will silence the voices of some San Franciscans forever. Citizens’ initiatives make a difference. They have increased the minimum wage, ensured large corporations pay their fair share of taxes, provided legal aid for renters facing eviction, banned corrupt contributions to politicians, passed Sunshine laws, established rent control, and funded schools, childcare and affordable housing. After 125 years of direct democracy, don’t let them rob it away. Vote NO on D.

arguments.heading: D ENDS THE INSIDER MONOPOLY ON POWER AT THE BALLOT
arguments.text: The insiders are misleading voters because their monopoly on power is being challenged. They think the system works great. San Franciscans know the system is broken: keeping us in a constant state of confusion, dividing neighbors, and producing bad outcomes. D is a set of modest reforms requiring transparency, compromise, and community input before issues get on the ballot so that voters can weigh in on well thought-out measures. None of these reforms add a financial cost. D REBALANCES POWER TO VOTERS Currently a minority of supervisors, just 2% of voters, or the mayor acting alone can throw anything on the ballot without public input, transparency, or proven community support. Political insiders exploit these rules regularly. That is why San Francisco has the longest and most confusing ballots in the state. D REQUIRES TRANSPARENCY, COMPROMISE AND COMMUNITY INPUT. With D, placing a measure on the ballot requires a public vote of a majority of the Supervisors or a modest amount of signatures. D also removes the mayor’s sole authority to place measures on the ballot, ensuring a fair balance of power. Opponents claim today’s rules date to 1932. The Controller’s report confirms the current threshold was set in 2022, requiring approximately 9,000 fewer signatures than before. San Francisco will still have one of the lowest signature thresholds in California, including other large cities like Oakland, San Diego, and Long Beach.

arguments.heading: Fewer Measures. Better Decisions.
arguments.text: San Francisco voters face some of the longest, most complicated ballots in California — 15 local measures in November 2024 alone, compared to 3 in Oakland and 1 in San José. Since 1996, San Franciscans have voted on 418 local measures, nearly half placed on the ballot without the ordinary legislative process of public hearings and Board approval. This reform comes straight from SPUR’s Charter for Change (2026), building on recommendations SPUR first raised in Designed to Serve (2024) and on SPUR’s long history of advocating for smarter, more deliberate lawmaking in San Francisco, including its sponsorship of 2007’s ballot-sunshine reforms. The measure ends the practice of the Mayor or just four Supervisors placing measures directly on the ballot without majority Board support — a power no other major California city grants. It raises the citizen signature threshold from 2% to 8% of registered voters, still lower than Oakland, San Diego, Sacramento, and most California cities. And it lets initiative sponsors withdraw measures before an election, opening the door to negotiated solutions instead of costly campaigns. Complex policy deserves public hearings and negotiation, not an up-or-down vote squeezed between a dozen other measures. This measure lets City Hall do its job, reserving the ballot for issues that truly need a public vote. Vote YES.

arguments.heading: GOOD GOVERNANCE LEADERS AGREE PROP D WILL IMPROVE VOTER TRUST.
arguments.text: A healthy democracy depends on a ballot voters can trust — one with proposals made with real community support, not political maneuvering. San Francisco’s current system falls far short. It requires 80% fewer signatures than the state standard, meaning a small minority of politicians and private interests can flood the ballot with contradictory measures designed to confuse voters and settle political scores. We’ve seen how this plays out: instead of building coalitions and answering hard questions publicly, insiders can target a handful of supervisors to get a measure on the ballot. Prop D protects the ballot from manipulation. It requires a majority of the Board of Supervisors or signatures from 8% of voters — much closer to the state’s 10% standard — and removes the mayor’s power to unilaterally place measures on the ballot, which no other California cities had to start with. It also lets proponents withdraw measures, allowing space to reach agreements or correct for flaws or unintended consequences instead of leaving voters to clean up the mess. This is a structural fix for a structural problem: a process that currently rewards insider access instead of genuine coalition-building and public vetting. Good government and a functioning democracy means a ballot voters can trust. Prop D gets us there.

arguments.heading: LABOR LEADERS SAY YES ON D FOR BETTER RESULTS AT THE BALLOT.
arguments.text: Working people don’t have lobbyists on retainer — we build power through coalitions, organizing, and showing up. San Francisco’s ballot process currently rewards the opposite. It makes it easy for a small group of politicians to put divisive, intentionally confusing measures forward without building real public support. Under the current system, private interests can skip community organizing altogether and just lobby a few supervisors to put measures before voters. Those with the most access use that shortcut instead of doing the work of earning broad support, the way labor always has. Prop D levels the playing field. A ballot process that rewards coalition-building over insider access is a ballot process that works better for working people and the organizations that represent us. Labor believes in earning support the real way. Vote Yes on Prop D for a fair, transparent democracy.

arguments.heading: Billionaires Buying Election Ballot Measures
arguments.text: “Proposition D” contains two poison pills: One eliminates four City Supervisors — a minority of the Board — from placing a measure on the ballot, increasing the requirement to six or more. That silences dissenting Supervisors, requiring majority unanimity. That’s undemocratic to voters and Supervisors not bought off by billionaires. The second raises the number of signatures required to qualify a citizen petition ballot initiative, from 2% to 8% of registered voters, a 300% increase, requiring 31,316 additional signatures to qualify, a potential $574,987 cost increase to $766,649, beyond San Francisco voter initiatives’ means. Through 7/15/2026, an Ethics Commission campaign finance dashboard (https://campaign.sfethics.org/elections/2026-11-03/committees/CA1489257.html) disclosed Mayor Lurie’s controlled ballot measure recipient committee “Clean Up City Hall” received $8.95 million from seven billionaires, centimillionaires, and multimillionaires, including Michael Moritz ($2M), Chris Larsen ($1M), Larsen’s wife Lyna Lam ($1M), and John Pritzker ($1M), among others. Of 21 donations, the smallest was $10,000, with zero $100-or-less small-dollar donations. They spent $4.9 million through 7/15/2026 collecting 245,744 signatures to qualify placing Propositions “D,” “E,” and “F” on the ballot, at approximately $18.35 per signature. The campaign finance pre-election report due 9/24/2026 will document additional revenue and expenditures. Billionaires are probably raising more money to buy passage of Lurie’s three signature ballot measures. Before voting, check their updated finance reports at https://netfile.com/public/sfo/campaign/filingsByFiler/216006060-Clean%20Up%20City%20Hall,%20Mayor%20Lurie’s%20Ballot%20Measure%20Committee. The $9 million raised through 7/15/2026 may double, to buy passage of “Proposition D”! City Supervisors are still considering raising paid ballot argument filing fees, and stopping publication of ballot measure legal text in voter guides, weakening voter education (see https://www.westsideobserver.net/26/7-lurie-voter-guide-overhaul-stalls.php). Our ballot measure process isn’t broken, doesn’t need fixing! Reign in Lurie’s billionaire club; kick outside billionaire money out of politics! Stop this insanity: Vote “No” on Propositions “A,” “D,” “E,” and “F”!

arguments.heading: 42,500 signatures: easy for wealthy interests, impossible for your neighborhood
arguments.text: If Prop D passes, it will require 42,500 signatures to place an ordinance on the ballot, four times higher than the 10,600 required today. Wealthy interests can use paid signature companies at a cost of $20 per signature or more – nearly $1 million. Neighbors and ordinary citizens would need up to 10,000 volunteer hours to collect the same amount. Prop D won’t stop ballot bloat – it will just let those who can write big checks put their measures on the ballot, while regular San Franciscans are left out. Protect access for everyone, and vote NO on D.

Protect access for everyone, and vote NO on D.

arguments.text: Big real estate interests are funding Prop D because it will prevent renters from passing laws to protect us from unfair evictions, excessive rent hikes and unscrupulous landlords. This required 9,485 signatures to get on the ballot and was passed by an overwhelming majority of voters. Wealthy interests are spending millions to pass Prop D to make the threshold an impossible 42,500 signatures and stop measures that protect renters. Vote No on D.

arguments.heading: Prop D takes away our tool to fight corruption in City Hall. No on D!
arguments.text: Prop D will take away an important tool for citizen-led reform, and give only the very wealthiest individuals and corporations the right to place measures on the ballot. Vote No on D. For decades, businesses with lucrative city contracts were allowed to contribute to the campaigns of politicians who approved those contracts. This conflict of interest benefited the contractors and the politicians, but taxpayers and citizens paid the cost. Then a group of citizens put Prop J on the ballot in 2000 to force reform at City Hall – needing 9,735 signatures to qualify. If Prop D passes, the next reform initiative would need 42,500 signatures – nearly impossible without spending $1 million or more.

arguments.heading: 42,500 signatures is easy for wealthy interests, impossible for everyone else. Vote No on D
arguments.text: Prop D is a dangerous measure that uses positive language — “streamlining, simplifying” — to obscure its true function: raising the signature threshold for citizen initiatives from 10,600 to 42,500, nearly quadrupling the effort and expense required to qualify a measure for the ballot. Deep-pocketed special interests who can afford professional signature-gathering firms will still be able to place initiatives on the ballot — even frivolous ones — while grassroots campaigns, labor unions, and community groups are locked out entirely. Since 1932, San Francisco has required an average of 10,000 signatures, giving citizens access to the ballot. Don’t let them take this vital safeguard away. No on D!

arguments.heading: PRESERVE CITIZEN DEMOCRACY-VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION
arguments.text: Is our initiative process “broken” because it allows citizens to persuade 10,600 voters (2% of registered voters) to petition for a ballot proposition? Should we “fix” this by requiring more nearly 42,500 signatures (8% of registered voters)? This increase will, undoubtedly, result in fewer citizen led initiatives. But corporations or dark-money PACs, who hire people to harvest signatures for their propositions, won’t be stopped. Do we really want to discourage citizen groups from even trying? Some say that our initiative process is “broken” because we allow ordinary citizens to vote on matters that may, to outsiders, seem trivial, such as closing a highway. The alternative view is that San Francisco is so democratic that we allow ordinary citizens to override bureaucrats on such matters of direct concern to the public. More than a hundred years ago, John Dewey famously said, “the cure for the ills of democracy is more democracy.” This proposal, however, argues that the solution is less democracy, less citizen involvement. I encourage you to vote NO.

proposal.value: Proposition D would amend the Charter to increase the requirements to put measures on the ballot by: • Increasing the number of signatures required to place a signature initiative on the ballot from 2% to 8% (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the registered voters in San Francisco. • Increasing the number of signatures required to call a special election on an ordinance from 10% of the votes cast for Mayor in the last election to 10% of the registered voters in San Francisco. Currently, this is about 53,100 signatures. Proposition D would allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn up to 102 days before the election. Proposition D would also change the requirements to put measures on the ballot by: • Removing the ability of four or more Board members to place a measure on the ballot without a Board vote; • Removing the ability of the Mayor to independently place a measure on the ballot; The Board could still place measures on the ballot by a majority vote.

way_it_is_now.value: The San Francisco Board of Supervisors (Board) has 11 members. A measure can be either an ordinance to change the law or a declaration of policy. Under the City Charter, measures can be placed on the ballot in several ways, including: • By a majority vote of the Board; • By four or more Board members without a Board vote; • By the Mayor without a Board vote; or • By a signature initiative (petition) signed by at least 2% of the registered voters in San Francisco, currently about 10,600 signatures. Currently San Francisco has over 530,000 registered voters. Signature initiatives usually appear on the ballot at the next regularly scheduled election. Signature initiatives may call for an earlier “special” election on an ordinance if the petition is signed by at least 10% of the votes cast for all candidates for Mayor in the last election. Currently, this is about 39,000 signatures. Once a signature initiative is submitted to the Department of Elections, it cannot be withdrawn.

It may result in a reduction in ballot ordinances which would reduce the associated workload for the Department of Elections— freeing staff to work on other government functions.
